title: Thoughts from the Road: Europe and Asia
summary: Over the past few weeks I spent time in London and Singapore meeting with politicians, policymakers, investors, business leaders, and clients. Learn more.
body_markdown:
Over the past few weeks I spent time in London and Singapore meeting with politicians, policymakers, investors, business leaders, and clients. I came away with several views that are different from when I started my journey. Most importantly, I now think that the global investment cycle is broader, more durable, and probably more inflationary than even I had appreciated. To be sure, AI remains an important growth driver (and we gained more confidence on the semiconductor cycle while in Asia), but Defense, Infrastructure, Energy, and supply chain resiliency are also now increasingly competing for the same capital, labor, and power.

So, not surprisingly, from a macro and asset allocation perspective, my travels only reinforced our *Regime Change* thesis. This cycle is increasingly being driven by fixed investment rather than leveraged consumption. More capital spending should continue to support greater productivity, real wages, and nominal growth, though it will create more cost of living headwinds. As such, this trip also confirmed our view that inflation and interest rates will continue to have a ‘higher resting heart rate’, which was not the case during the era of Secular Stagnation. Finally, heightened geopolitics are leading to more economic choke points being leveraged for political gains than in the past.


Armed with these findings and data points from the trip, we are using this *Thoughts From the Road* to raise several of our short- and long-rate forecasts. One can see this in *Exhibit 4* . In terms of specifics, on the long end, we are lifting 10-Year forecasts for the bund, gilt, and JGB, while also increasing our forecast for 2026 ECB and Bank of England short-term interest rates. Importantly, the breadth of the investment boom is part of what is driving that change in our thinking.


**EXHIBIT 3: Around the World, CEOs View Supply Chain Disruptions and Geopolitical Uncertainties as Elevated Risks in 2026**


Based on 771 CEOs responding. Source: The Conference Board, C-Suite Outlook 2026: Uncertainty and Opportunity (2026), https://www.conference-board.org/publications/C-Suite-Outlook-2026-Uncertainty-and-Opportunity.


Somewhat ironically, though, I am not convinced that higher-for-longer means higher forever. Indeed, I came home less convinced that markets are currently right to price in a long, consistent, unwavering series of near-term hikes. To this end, I note that forward curves around the globe now appear as disconnected to the upside from KKR’s forecast in the out years as we have seen in quite some time (see Section I for more details).


**EXHIBIT 4: Renewed Inflation, Fiscal Pressures and Continued Policy Normalization Are Pushing Our Global Rate Forecasts Modestly Higher**


Data as at September 29, 2026. Source: KKR Global Macro & Asset Allocation analysis.


I also came away from this trip even more focused on the widening gaps across countries, companies, and consumers. In particular, cost-of-living pressures remain meaningful for lower- and middle-income households everywhere. This cruel reality is not just a developed market or developing market story, and it is prevalent across the U.S., the U.K., Singapore, and even India and Malaysia. At the same time, many large companies and asset owners are benefiting from higher investment, greater productivity, and higher profits. One can see this in *Exhibit 5* . This particular disconnect remains central to our overall Divergence Conundrum thesis, which we detailed in our Mid-Year Outlook (See[The Divergence Conundrum](https://www.kkr.com/insights/mid-year-update-2026) ).

So, what changed in my thinking after all this travel? Beyond the idea that we need to boost our rates forecast, six things stood out:


**1. The global investment boom is broader than I thought.** AI is only one part of a much larger spending cycle that now includes Defense, Infrastructure, Energy, and supply-chain resiliency. This strengthens our conviction that nominal growth, inflation, and rates will have a ‘higher resting heart rate’ than they did during Secular Stagnation.


**2. Europe is more resilient than I expected, but the composition of growth matters.** Specifically, Business Investment, Defense, Infrastructure, and regional trade are increasingly doing more of the work, while consumers and housing remain constrained. Germany is now trading more with Eastern Europe and less with China, and countries like the U.K. are seeing a surge in business fixed investment, even as traditional capital expenditures such as housing lag.


**3. The next 12 months in Europe will bring an action-packed political agenda and election calendar, with some potential concerns already being reflected in government bond markets.** Without question, we are closely watching bond yields in France; we do not see the risk as a 2011-redo, as there are more safeguards in place today. However, the path ahead will not be easy, as budgets need to be tightened, which is hard to do during election season. On the corporate side, we would use any dislocations linked to government sovereignty issues to increase exposure to some of our most important regional investment themes, including the Resurgence of the Periphery, Retirement Savings, Renewables, and the Security of Everything.


**4. In Asia, the AI opportunity is broader than chips.** Japan, in particular, reinforced for me how much value sits upstream in equipment, materials, chemicals, power, and related infrastructure. Just consider that in 2025 AI-affiliated activities in Japan accounted for less than 3% of GDP but contributed more than 20% of the country’s GDP growth.


**5. Korea’s corporate reform story looks even more investable than it did before this trip.** We spent more time discussing reform in Korea than Japan, which itself was a notable change from prior visits. We also heard of incremental improvements in the Singapore story, especially as it relates to financial services.


**6. Global allocators want more exposure to Asia, especially across Infrastructure, Equities (both Public and Private), and Credit. Yet, their allocations are still below their benchmarks, we believe.** Until recently, the change in China’s trajectory over the past decade dominated investor thinking. However, many are now looking for ways to invest behind the region’s mega themes, including Intra-Asia Trade, Consumption Upgrades, Corporate Reform, AI-enablers, and Decarbonization. Therein lies the opportunity, we believe.
